bib.title: ON THE THEORETICAL LIMITATIONS OF EMBEDDING-BASED RETRIEVAL

question: What is the fundamental limit on which top-k document sets a single-vector embedding of dimension d can return, and do state-of-the-art embedders hit it on realistic simple queries?
hypothesis: Embedding dimension limits the number of top-k subsets that can be returned, so even simple queries over all combinations of relevance will defeat single-vector models.
contributions: a theoretical basis for the fundamental limitations of embedding models
a best-case empirical analysis showing that this proof holds for any dataset instantiation (by free embedding optimization)
a simple real-world natural language instantiation called LIMIT that even state-of-the-art embedding models cannot solve

method.summary: A sphere-packing lower bound on embedding dimension for realizing all k-subsets with a margin; a free-embedding optimisation experiment (k=2) finding the critical corpus size per dimension; and the LIMIT dataset (50k docs, 1000 'who likes X' queries) evaluated on single-vector, multi-vector and sparse retrievers, plus a fine-tuning control for domain shift.

limits: Theory is for single-vector embeddings; does not necessarily hold for multi-vector models (Limitations).
No bound for the setting where some mistakes are allowed.
Cannot prove a priori which combinations models fail on; some tasks may be solved perfectly.
Free-embedding critical n measured only for d=4 to 45; larger d is cubic extrapolation.
Bound assumes unit vectors, dot product, and a fixed margin; the sign-rank result in Appendix D without margin is weaker.
LIMIT is synthetic with one instantiation; single run, no seeds or significance tests; Gemini reranker prompt not given.
Appendix C: sigmoid loss (Bangachev et al.) can solve free embeddings in fewer dimensions, so learnability questions remain.
Lexical models are not a panacea: BM25 drops most under synonyms.
